passage: Every morning the sabziwala pushed his cart through the colony calling, “Aaloo-pyaaz-tamaaaatar!” By the third week, Jeevan was chanting it too from the balcony, in exactly the same tune, drumming the railing. Then he did the pressure cooker: “Shhhh-WHEEE!” and the doorbell: “Ding-dong-ding!” Jasleen, his mother, laughed from the kitchen. One morning the sabziwala looked up and grinned. “Arre, my helper!” He called, and Jeevan called back. They sang the whole list together, and Jeevan bounced on his toes.

qa.q: What did the sabziwala call out?
qa.a: “Aaloo-pyaaz-tamaaaatar!”

qa.q: What was Jeevan feeling as he chanted with the sabziwala?
qa.a: He was joyful and excited, enjoying the tune and the shared game, which is why he bounced on his toes.

qa.q: How could Jasleen build on Jeevan's love of copying sounds?
qa.a: She could play sound games with him, like guessing household sounds or making up chants, to support his language and joy.

qa.q: How did the sabziwala see Jeevan's copying?
qa.a: He took it as friendly play, not mockery, and even called Jeevan his helper.

grounding: A preschooler chants a vendor's call and copies household sounds as play, and the vendor joins in.

passage:
“Moo! Baa! Quack!” Sahil galloped round the room.
Kalyani Didi laughed. “Do the lion!”
“ROAR!”
Then Sahil said, “Now I'm Ravi.” He screwed up his mouth. “Thith ith my thchool.”
Kalyani stopped laughing. “Wait. Is that playing, or teasing?”
Sahil paused. “…Teasing. Everyone does it.”
“How would Ravi feel if he heard?”
Sahil looked at his feet. “Sad.”
“Animals are fun to copy. People's voices, not to hurt.”
“Okay.” He brightened. “Can I be a train instead? Choo choo!”

qa.q: Which animal sounds did Sahil make first?
qa.a: Moo, baa and quack.

qa.q: What was Sahil feeling when he looked at his feet?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and sorry once he imagined Ravi hearing the copied lisp and feeling sad.

qa.q: How did Kalyani Didi help Sahil see the difference?
qa.a: She asked whether it was playing or teasing and how Ravi would feel, so Sahil worked it out himself.

qa.q: What is it like for Ravi when others copy his voice?
qa.a: It would likely feel hurtful and humiliating, since the copying is aimed at him.

grounding: A preschooler imitates animals in play and then a classmate's speech, and his sister helps him see when imitation hurts.

passage:

passage:
Creche note by Sudha, evening carer.
Damini's mother was late today, delayed by traffic. At six, Damini sat in the book corner, holding her teddy, and began to sing very softly: “Chanda mama door ke…” over and over, rocking. She wasn't crying. I didn't interrupt; it seemed to be helping her. After a while she held the teddy out to me and said, “Teddy wants you to sing too.” So I sang with them. When her mother arrived, Damini was humming and calm.

qa.q: Why was Damini's mother late?
qa.a: She was delayed by traffic.

qa.q: What was Damini feeling as she sang to her teddy?
qa.a: She was probably lonely and a little worried that her mother was late, and singing helped her feel calm.

qa.q: Why was Sudha right not to interrupt?
qa.a: Singing was Damini's own healthy way of coping, and Sudha joined in only when Damini invited her.

qa.q: How might Damini's mother feel reading this note?
qa.a: She would likely feel relieved and grateful that Damini found a way to stay calm and that Sudha supported her.

grounding: The carer's note shows a preschooler singing softly to her teddy to soothe herself, and the carer joining when invited.

passage: In the evening, Seema went to milk the buffalo behind the house, and Sahil stayed on the charpai in the courtyard. The lamp flickered. The fields were dark and full of croaking. Sahil pulled his blanket tight and started singing, “Machhli jal ki rani hai,” softly to himself, then a little louder. From the shed came Seema's voice, singing the next line. Sahil sang the line after. They went back and forth until she came out with the warm milk bucket and sat beside him.

qa.q: Where did Seema go in the evening?
qa.a: To milk the buffalo behind the house.

qa.q: What was Sahil feeling when he pulled his blanket tight and began singing?
qa.a: He was probably a bit scared and lonely in the dark courtyard, and singing helped him soothe himself.

qa.q: What did Seema's singing back do for Sahil?
qa.a: It let him know she was near and joined his coping song, so he felt less alone.

qa.q: What would change if Seema had called out “Stop singing, be quiet”?
qa.a: Sahil would lose his way of calming himself and might feel more frightened.

grounding: A child sings to soothe himself when alone and uneasy in the dark, and his mother joins in from nearby.

passage: The drive to Galway took three hours, and the rain didn't stop. In the back seat, Rafael had run out of games. qa.q: How long did the drive to Galway take?
qa.a: Three hours.

qa.q: What was Rafael feeling when he began singing to the dinosaur?
qa.a: He was bored after running out of games, and singing helped him cope with the long, rainy drive.

qa.q: What did Liam do that honoured Rafael's singing?
qa.a: He turned the radio off to listen and waited until Rafael invited him before joining in.

qa.q: How might Liam feel when Rafael invites him to sing?
qa.a: He likely feels touched and happy to be let in, which is why he sings the next verse in a deep dino voice. 😊

grounding: A child sings to his toy to soothe boredom on a long drive, and his father joins in when invited.

passage: The wedding hall was crowded and loud, and Manoj had only a minute before the photos. He spotted his boss. “Pradeep, say hello to Sharma Sir. He'll say hello when he's ready.” Later, at the food counter, Pradeep took a plate from a waiter and whispered, “Thank you.” Manoj squeezed his shoulder.

qa.q: What did Pradeep whisper at the food counter?
qa.a: “Thank you.”

qa.q: What was Pradeep feeling when he pressed his face into Manoj's side?
qa.a: He was shy and overwhelmed by the crowded, loud hall and a stranger asking for his name.

qa.q: Which choice by Manoj worked, and why?
qa.a: He respected Pradeep's shyness instead of pushing, and Pradeep later said thank you on his own.

qa.q: How did the moment feel for Manoj?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed in front of his boss but chose to protect Pradeep's comfort.

grounding: A preschooler goes quiet and hides when prompted to greet a stranger, his father respects it, and later he says thank you.

passage: New neighbours moved into the flat opposite. Tarun's mother knocked with a plate of laddoos, Tarun holding the edge. A tall man opened the door. Tarun's mother whispered, “Say hello and your name.” Tarun took a breath. “Hello. I'm Tarun. I'm five.” The man bent down. “Hello, Tarun. I'm Deepak. qa.a: Laddoos.

qa.q: What was Tarun feeling when he said, “I did it all by myself. Almost”?
qa.a: He felt proud of greeting Deepak, while honestly noticing that his mother's prompts had helped.

qa.q: What small step helped Tarun greet the new neighbour?
qa.a: His mother's quiet prompt, “Say hello and your name,” and her nod helped him know what to say.

qa.q: How might Deepak feel being greeted by Tarun?
qa.a: He likely feels welcomed and pleased by the friendly introduction from a new neighbour.

grounding: A preschooler learns to say hello, give his name and say you're welcome with adult prompting.

passage:
“Remember what we say at the shop?” Noor Khala asked on the stairs.
“Hello,” said Yusuf.
“And if they ask your name?”
“My name is Yusuf.”
“And when he gives the sweets?”
“Um…”
“Thank…”
“Thank you!”
At the counter, the shopkeeper said, “Hello, young man. What's your name?” Yusuf looked at Khala, swallowed, and said very quietly, “Yusuf.” The shopkeeper handed over the sweets. Yusuf whispered, “Thank you.” Outside, Khala hugged him. “Perfect.” “I forgot hello,” he said. “Next time.”

qa.q: What did the shopkeeper hand over?
qa.a: The sweets.

qa.q: What was Yusuf feeling at the counter when he spoke very quietly?
qa.a: He was nervous and shy with the shopkeeper, though he still wanted to try what he had practised.

qa.q: What helped Yusuf say his name and thank you?
qa.a: Noor Khala practised the words with him on the stairs and prompted him gently.

qa.q: How might Noor Khala see Yusuf forgetting hello?
qa.a: She sees it as normal and is proud of what he managed, which is why she said “Perfect” and hugged him.

grounding: A preschooler practises greeting, giving his name and saying thank you with an adult's prompting.

passage:
Grandparents' Day note, from Suraj, KG teacher.
Today several children touched their grandparents' feet when they arrived. Zubin stood still, unsure, while his grandmother waited. A boy said, “Why didn't you touch her feet? That's rude!” Zubin's face went red. I said, “Families greet in different ways. Some touch feet, some say namaste, some hug, some say salaam.” Zubin's grandmother opened her arms, and Zubin ran into a hug. Later the class shared how each family greets elders.

qa.q: What did some children do when their grandparents arrived?
qa.a: They touched their grandparents' feet.

qa.q: What was Zubin feeling when his face went red?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and ashamed when the boy called him rude, and unsure what he was supposed to do.

qa.q: How did Suraj respond to the boy's comment?
qa.a: Suraj explained kindly that families greet in different ways, so Zubin was not shamed.

qa.q: How might the boy who said “rude” see greetings after the class sharing?
qa.a: He might learn that there are many respectful ways to greet elders, not only the one his family uses.

grounding: The teacher's note shows a child unsure how to greet an elder, and the teacher explaining that customs vary rather than shaming him.

passage: Zainab went home with her friend after school, in their small town. Her friend's Dadi was on the porch, and her friend bent down and touched Dadi's feet. Zainab stood holding her bag, not sure what to do. Swati, her friend's mother, noticed. “Zainab, beta, you can greet Dadi however your family does.” Zainab thought. “At home I say adaab.” She raised her hand to her forehead. “Adaab, Dadi.” Dadi smiled and did the same back. “Adaab, beti. Come, have some sherbet.”

qa.q: How did Zainab greet Dadi?
qa.a: She raised her hand to her forehead and said, “Adaab, Dadi.”

qa.q: What was Zainab feeling as she stood holding her bag?
qa.a: She was unsure and a little nervous about how to greet Dadi, since her friend's custom was different from hers.

qa.q: What did Swati say that helped?
qa.a: She told Zainab she could greet Dadi however her family does, so Zainab didn't feel she had to copy.

qa.q: How might Dadi see Zainab's adaab?
qa.a: She took it as a warm, respectful greeting and returned it, showing respect across customs.

grounding: A child unsure of another family's custom is taught kindly that she can greet the elder in her own family's way.

passage: At her friend Priyanka's Diwali party in Johannesburg, Zanele watched Priyanka bend and touch her grandfather's feet. Zanele wanted to do it too. qa.a: Her friend Priyanka's Diwali party.

qa.q: What was Zanele feeling when her cheeks burned?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed when everyone laughed, worried she had done it wrong.

qa.q: What did Priyanka's grandfather do that taught kindly?

grounding: A child tries touching an elder's feet at a friend's party and is taught kindly that another greeting is fine too.

passage: In the KG room, Rajni Ma'am asked Baljeet about his drawing. “This is a car and… the sun… no, first we went to the shop, and the dog was barking and then… my cousin.” He stopped, frowning at the page. qa.q: What was Baljeet feeling when he stopped and frowned at the page?

grounding: A preschooler describes his drawing with gaps and mixed-up order, and his teacher's patient prompts help him tell it.

passage: I'm Chetan, Vandana's brother. After play, Vandana ran in to tell Mummy what happened. “Riya fell and there was blood, no, first we were on the slide, and then the ball, and she cried, and I gave her my hanky.” Mummy didn't say, “That's not making sense.” She said, “You were on the slide. qa.q: What might Vandana have been feeling as she told the story?

passage:
Monday: Ankita told Yamini, her mother, about school: “We had lunch, and then circle, and first the bus…” Yamini said, “No, the bus is first, you've got it wrong.” Ankita stopped and said, “Never mind.”
Wednesday: Ankita started again with a jumble. Yamini waited, then asked, “And what happened first?” “The bus!” “And then what?” Ankita told it all.
Friday: Ankita came in and said, “First the bus, then circle, then lunch, then a bee came in!” Yamini gasped, “A bee! And then what?”

qa.q: What came in on Friday?
qa.a: A bee.

qa.q: What was Ankita feeling when she said “Never mind” on Monday?
qa.a: She felt discouraged and a bit embarrassed at being told she had got it wrong, so she gave up.

qa.q: What changed on Wednesday that helped Ankita?
qa.a: Yamini stopped correcting and used patient prompts like “what happened first?” and “And then what?”

qa.q: How might Yamini feel on Friday?
qa.a: She likely feels happy and proud that Ankita now tells her stories eagerly and in order.

grounding: Over a week, a mother learns that patient prompts help her preschooler's reports more than correcting her order.

passage: I'm Irfan, Mridul's big brother. Yesterday Mridul told the neighbour aunty, “A lion came to our school and I fed it a biscuit!” Aunty's eyes went wide. Mummy smiled. “Was it a pretend lion or a real one?” Mridul thought. “A real cat. But it was big like a lion.” Mummy said, “What a great story. And a real cat came to school!” I don't know if Mridul thought it was really a lion, but he wasn't told off.

qa.q: What did Mridul say he fed the lion?
qa.a: A biscuit.

qa.q: What might Mridul have been feeling as he told the lion story?
qa.a: He was probably excited about the cat at school and wanted his story to be as big as his feelings. Irfan isn't sure if he believed it was a lion.

qa.q: How did Mummy separate pretend from real without a harsh label?
qa.a: She asked if it was a pretend lion or a real one, and praised the story while noting that a real cat came.

qa.q: How might the neighbour aunty have seen the lion story?
qa.a: She was surprised at first, then probably amused when she heard it was a big cat.

grounding: A brother observes a preschooler blend fantasy with fact, and their mother gently separates pretend from real.

passage:

qa.a: She likely feels pleased and amused that Rekha is learning to mark pretend from real herself.

grounding: Over a week, a mother enjoys her child's fantasy stories but gently checks what is real when safety matters.

passage: Construction drilling rattled the classroom windows all morning. Noor Ma'am gave instructions for the craft: “Fold the paper, cut the corner, then glue it on the blue sheet.” Most children started. Divyansh sat still, then raised his hand. “I don't understand. Say it again?” Noor walked over, knelt beside him and said it slowly, one step at a time. Then she said to the class, “Divyansh did a smart thing. qa.a: Construction drilling.

qa.q: What was Divyansh feeling when he sat still before raising his hand?
qa.a: He was probably confused and unsure, because he hadn't understood the instructions over the noise.

grounding: In a noisy classroom, a child asks for the instruction again, and the teacher praises asking so no one feels shame.

passage:
“Omkar, go get your jumper, it's cold,” said Joseph.
Omkar ran to his room and came back with his skipping rope.
Joseph laughed, then saw Omkar's face fall. “Not a jumping rope. A jumper, like a sweater.”
Omkar went pink. “I didn't know.”
“That's okay. What could you say next time?”
Omkar thought. “What is a jumper?”
“Exactly. Asking is clever.”
Omkar fetched his sweater, pulled it on, and then asked, “What is a scarf?”
Joseph grinned. “Good question.”

qa.a: His skipping rope.

qa.q: What was Omkar feeling when he went pink?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed about getting it wrong and a bit hurt when his father laughed.

qa.q: How did Joseph turn the mistake into learning?
qa.a: He noticed Omkar's face, explained the word, and taught him to ask “What is a jumper?” next time, praising asking.

qa.q: How might Joseph feel when Omkar asks about the scarf?
qa.a: He is likely pleased and amused, glad that Omkar feels safe to ask.

grounding: A child guesses wrong about a word, and his father teaches and praises asking for clarification instead.

passage:

passage: On the tram in Berlin, Tomas pressed his nose to the window. “Why is the tram on lines?” “So it knows where to go,” said Zeynep, his mother. “Why?” “Because it can't steer like a car.” “Why?” Zeynep smiled, tired. “What do you think?” Tomas thought hard. “Because… it's too long to turn by itself?” “Good thinking.” “Why is that dog on the tram?” Zeynep laughed. “Maybe he's going to the park. qa.q: How might Zeynep feel after many whys on the tram?

grounding: A preschooler asks endless why questions on a tram, and his mother keeps the talk going with short answers and asking what he thinks.

passage: At the preschool, Jyoti Ma'am was watering the plants. qa.q: How might Jyoti see Rajni's whys?

grounding: A preschooler asks why again and again, partly testing limits, and the teacher asks what she thinks and involves her.

passage: I'm Vandana, Amandeep's neighbour. “Dinosaurs live in the park,” Pranav said firmly.
“Really?” asked Anjali, his mother.
“Yes. Behind the big tree. I heard one.”
“Hmm. I don't know about that. What did it sound like?”
“Grrrr.”
“That could be a dinosaur. Or a dog. I'm not sure. How can we find out?”

“Let's go and look.”

Note by Pankaj, preschool teacher.
During nature walk, Rafiq told the group, “Spiders are insects. My brother said.” He was very sure. Another child said they weren't. Rafiq folded his arms. I said, “I'm not sure. Let's find out together.” Back in class we looked in the bug book. Spiders have eight legs; insects have six. Rafiq counted the legs in the picture twice. “Eight,” he said slowly. “So not insects.” I told him, “I didn't know for sure either. Now we both know.”

qa.q: How many legs do spiders have, according to the bug book?
qa.a: Eight.

qa.q: What was Rafiq feeling when he folded his arms?
qa.a: He felt certain and a bit defensive when another child disagreed, since his brother had told him.

qa.q: What did Pankaj model that helped Rafiq accept the answer?
qa.a: Pankaj said “I'm not sure, let's find out,” and later admitted not knowing for sure either, showing uncertainty is fine.

qa.q: How might the child who disagreed feel after the book?
qa.a: That child might feel pleased to be right, but the teacher's way of checking together kept it from being a win over Rafiq.

grounding: The teacher's note shows a preschooler certain of a fact, and the teacher modelling “I'm not sure, let's find out.”

passage: I'm Deepika, Gopika's sister. When Mummy told Gopika her wobbly tooth would fall out and a new one would grow, Gopika's eyes went huge. “Really? No way!” Then she said, “And when it falls, the tooth fairy will bring me a bicycle. It will be big!” Mummy smiled. “We hope for nice things. But I don't know about a bicycle. What we do know is a new tooth will grow.” Gopika wiggled her tooth. I couldn't tell if she was disappointed or still hoping.

qa.q: What did Gopika say the tooth fairy would bring?
qa.a: A bicycle.

qa.q: What might Gopika have been feeling when her eyes went huge?
qa.a: She was probably amazed and surprised, perhaps a little doubtful, that a tooth could fall out and grow again.

qa.q: How did Mummy separate hope from what is known?
qa.a: She said it's fine to hope for nice things, but she didn't know about a bicycle, while a new tooth growing was known.

qa.q: How does Deepika see Gopika after Mummy's answer?
qa.a: Deepika can't tell whether Gopika is disappointed or still hoping, noticing she keeps wiggling the tooth.

grounding: A sister observes a preschooler's disbelief and big expectation about a tooth, and their mother gently separates hope from fact.

passage:
March: The mango tree flowered. Farhan announced, “There will be a hundred mangoes! It will be big!” Rafiq, his father, said, “We'll see. I hope so too.”
April: Rafiq showed him tiny green mangoes where the flowers had been. “No way! Really?” Farhan's eyes went wide. “Flowers turn into mangoes?” “Really.”
June: They counted the ripe mangoes. Twelve. Farhan's face fell. “Not a hundred.” Rafiq hugged him. “You hoped for a hundred. We didn't know. Twelve sweet ones is what we got.”

qa.q: How many ripe mangoes did they count in June?
qa.a: Twelve.

qa.q: What was Farhan feeling when his face fell in June?
qa.a: He was disappointed, because he had expected a hundred mangoes and treated his hope as if it were certain.

qa.q: What did Rafiq say that helped separate hope from what is known?
qa.a: He reminded Farhan that he had hoped for a hundred but they hadn't known, and that twelve sweet ones is what they got.

qa.q: How might Rafiq feel watching Farhan's wide eyes in April?
qa.a: He probably feels warm and amused, enjoying Farhan's amazement that flowers turn into mangoes.

grounding: Over months, a child expresses disbelief and big expectations about the mango tree, and his father gently separates hope from what is known.

passage: The monsoon clouds had been black all morning, and the village fair was supposed to start at four. Sumit sat at the door in his new shirt. “It will stop. It will be the biggest fair ever!” Zeenat Phuppo looked at the sky. “We all hope it stops. But we don't know yet.” Thunder rolled. Sumit's eyes went wide. “No way. Really raining more?” Phuppo sat beside him. “If it rains, we'll go tomorrow. If it stops, we'll run.” At half past three, the rain stopped.

qa.q: What time was the fair supposed to start?
qa.a: At four.

qa.q: What was Sumit feeling when thunder rolled and his eyes went wide?
qa.a: He felt disbelief and worry that the rain might spoil his hope of going to the fair.

qa.q: Which choice by Zeenat Phuppo worked, and why?
qa.a: She said everyone hoped it would stop but they didn't know, and gave a plan for both cases, which helped Sumit handle not knowing.

qa.q: What would change if Phuppo had promised the rain would stop?
qa.a: If it hadn't stopped, Sumit would have felt let down and confused about what was promised.

grounding: A child states a hopeful expectation about the fair despite the rain, and his aunt gently separates hope from what is known.
